scenes.tts: Chapter one showed that the energy hill sets which way a solute moves. So how can data reveal whether it crossed through a channel or a carrier? Watch the traffic, not the protein's name.
scenes.visual: Carry chapter one's world forward: a thick horizontal membrane band, pale-blue outside above, warm-tan inside below, and slowly jittering solute dots. Reuse orange for potassium, grey for sodium, yellow for glucose, and teal for voltage or measurement. Two blue membrane blocks, both labelled 'unknown', occupy the same opening in successive halves of the frame. Yellow solute dots cross both, so direction alone gives no answer. A large question mark grows between the blocks while a teal detector trace begins drawing at the right. The membrane and dots fill at least 60 percent of frame height.
scenes.narration: Chapter one showed that the energy hill sets which way a solute moves. So how can data reveal whether it crossed through a channel or a carrier? Watch the traffic, not the protein's name.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Read the Traffic' appears over the same membrane world. Solute dots keep jittering and the teal trace keeps extending behind the title. Hold for no more than two seconds.

scenes.tts: An open channel is a continuous pore between both sides. Ions stream through without waiting for a transport cycle. A channel can switch between open and closed; a carrier must finish each alternating-access cycle. A carrier opens to one side, closes around its solute, then opens to the other. That shape change limits each trip.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the membrane opening. The first blue block parts to reveal a continuous pale-blue pore; orange potassium dots stream through in single file. Then the block transforms, without a cut, into a blue carrier shaped like a cup. The cup opens above, catches one yellow solute chip, closes around it, then rocks into a second shape that opens below (the cup never turns over or moves through the membrane), and releases it. Label the two states only when named: 'continuous pore' and 'alternating access'. Mark the cartoon 'schematic'. Ambient dots keep moving.
scenes.narration: An open channel is a continuous pore between both sides. Ions stream through without waiting for a transport cycle. A channel can switch between open and closed; a carrier must finish each alternating-access cycle. A carrier opens to one side, closes around its solute, then opens to the other. That shape change limits each trip.

scenes.tts: A single channel gives the detector square current steps. Millions of ions per second can cross one pore, producing measurable current. Each jump marks an opening. The step height is the unitary current through one open channel. The fraction of recording time spent open is its open probability. Those are different measurements.
scenes.visual: Keep the channel at left and grow a large detector screen at right. A computed square trace draws left to right: zero while the pore is shut, then a fixed-height teal plateau while it opens. The gate moves in exact sync with each rise and fall. A vertical brace labels 'unitary current' beside one step. A horizontal timeline underneath fills green only during openings, then resolves into 'open time / total time'. No static axis labels beyond these two readouts.
scenes.narration: A single channel gives the detector square current steps. Millions of ions per second can cross one pore, producing measurable current. Each jump marks an opening. The step height is the unitary current through one open channel. The fraction of recording time spent open is its open probability. Those are different measurements.

scenes.tts: Now a drug makes the openings last longer, but every step keeps the same height. What changed: current through one open channel, or open probability? Decide from the trace.
scenes.visual: Stack two computed one-channel traces on the detector: 'before' above and 'drug' below. Both steps have identical height; the drug trace has wider plateaus while the closed gaps between openings keep the same lengths, so it spends visibly more of the time open. Place a pulsing question mark beside two answer chips: 'step height?' and 'time open?'. The channel gate continues opening and closing beside the traces.
scenes.narration: Now a drug makes the openings last longer, but every step keeps the same height. What changed: current through one open channel, or open probability? Decide from the trace.

scenes.visual: Hold both traces and the two answer chips. The question mark pulses slowly, the trace cursor advances, and the channel gate continues its matching motion. Near-silence.

scenes.tts: Open probability increased: the channel spent more of its time open. Unchanged step height means unchanged unitary current at this voltage. A whole-cell current alone mixes channel number, unitary current, and open probability, so it cannot separate them.
scenes.visual: The 'time open?' chip turns green and expands into a fraction bar whose numerator grows. The equal-height braces on both traces glow together, then the 'step height?' chip fades. Pull back to show many identical channels feeding one combined whole-cell trace. Three sliders labelled 'number', 'step', and 'time open' move in compensating directions while the same mean-current gauge holds steady. Mark the multi-channel cartoon 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Open probability increased: the channel spent more of its time open. Unchanged step height means unchanged unitary current at this voltage. A whole-cell current alone mixes channel number, unitary current, and open probability, so it cannot separate them.

scenes.tts: Carriers leave a different signature. Raise substrate concentration and their limited binding sites become occupied. The rate bends toward a ceiling called V max. A pore or simple diffusion can stay nearly proportional over the tested range. Channels can saturate too, usually only at much higher concentrations. Saturation points toward a carrier, but it is evidence, not proof.

scenes.visual: The many channels transform into matched membrane vesicles containing either blue carrier blocks or blue pore blocks. Yellow substrate outside rises from sparse to crowded. At right, compute and draw two labelled rate curves from the lesson's teaching functions: 'carrier', v = 60 times S divided by the quantity 1 plus S, bends toward 60; 'pore', v = 2.5 times S, stays linear from 0 to 20 millimolar. Show points at 1, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 millimolar. Do not use the lesson's table values or the names A and B: the text's Predict box tests those. Label axes 'substrate' and 'initial rate'; label the plot 'teaching data'. The carrier cycles continuously as its curve draws.

A pore or simple diffusion can stay nearly proportional over the tested range. Channels can saturate too, usually only at much higher concentrations. Saturation points toward a carrier, but it is evidence, not proof.

scenes.tts: Tracer experiments add a detectable tag to some substrate molecules. The counter sees tagged molecules entering, not the total amount inside. Take carrier vesicles with substrate already equal inside and outside. Add tagged substrate outside. Tagged molecules enter as untagged ones leave, so the total inside stays the same. A chemical assay of total substrate supplies what the tracer counter lacks.
scenes.visual: Transform the plot into one large vesicle. Yellow untagged dots sit at the same density inside and outside, and a label reads 'equal inside and outside'. Then some outside dots gain small teal tag badges. The carrier cups in the membrane cycle continuously, each trip carrying one dot either way, so tagged dots drift in while untagged dots drift out. A teal 'tag count' gauge rises while a white 'total inside' gauge stays level. Label the cartoon 'schematic'. Do not show a second, unloaded vesicle or any preloading: the text's Predict box tests that experiment.
scenes.narration: Tracer experiments add a detectable tag to some substrate molecules. The counter sees tagged molecules entering, not the total amount inside. Take carrier vesicles with substrate already equal inside and outside. Add tagged substrate outside. Tagged molecules enter as untagged ones leave, so the total inside stays the same. A chemical assay of total substrate supplies what the tracer counter lacks.

scenes.tts: That is exchange, not net uptake. Label has its own concentration difference, so it can run in while total substrate stays level. A rising count alone never proves accumulation. So measure the total, and combine exchange with rate, saturation, and single-channel steps instead of trusting one clue.
scenes.visual: Keep the vesicle large. The entering tagged dot and leaving untagged dot balance on a seesaw labelled 'one in / one out'; the total gauge remains level while the tag gauge keeps rising. Then split the detector into four moving evidence tiles around the same vesicle: a fast counter, a bending rate curve, paired exchange arrows, and a square current step. The tiles converge into one blue outline labelled 'mechanism'. Put a small caution triangle beside the counter tile on 'never proves'. All icons are labelled blocks or computed curves, never molecular structures.
scenes.narration: That is exchange, not net uptake. Label has its own concentration difference, so it can run in while total substrate stays level. A rising count alone never proves accumulation. So measure the total, and combine exchange with rate, saturation, and single-channel steps instead of trusting one clue.

scenes.tts: The hill from chapter one tells you which way traffic can run. The pattern of that traffic reveals the route. Square steps point to a pore. Saturation and exchange point toward a carrier. Mechanism lives in the measurements, not the family name.
scenes.visual: Return to the opening membrane world. Chapter one's white energy hill appears above two unknown blue blocks, then slides upward into a small header. Below it, the square trace, bending curve, and exchange arrows attach to their matching pore or carrier block. The question mark between the blocks resolves into a detector checkmark. The two routes keep moving solute in their distinct ways while the final sentence lands.
scenes.narration: The hill from chapter one tells you which way traffic can run. The pattern of that traffic reveals the route. Square steps point to a pore. Saturation and exchange point toward a carrier. Mechanism lives in the measurements, not the family name.

scenes.visual: End card over the softly moving membrane world: 'Read the traffic pattern, not the protein's label.' The pore streams and the carrier cycles slowly behind the line.
